The data doesn't back the idea that churn is mostly an onboarding problem. Most churn tracks the July 2025 price-increase notice, and onboarding has only a small effect.

| | Churn rate | Share of the 487 churned accounts it explains |
|---|---|---|
| Got the price-increase notice | 34.2% (vs 5.2% without) | about 68%, roughly 330 accounts |
| Did not finish onboarding | 17.6% (vs 15.2% for those who did) | at most about 6%, roughly 30 accounts |

- **Price notice:** 80% of churned accounts received it. The gap appears in every plan and every signup month.
- **Onboarding, with the notice held constant:** among accounts without the notice, the gap is 2.2 points (p = 0.03). Among accounts with it, the gap is 1.8 points (p = 0.52), and accounts that finished onboarding still churn at 33%.
- **Other columns:** plan, seats and signup month explain almost nothing. Support tickets rise with churn mostly among accounts that got the notice, so they look like a symptom of the price change rather than a separate cause.
- **Exit survey:** the "68% said onboarding was confusing" figure comes from churned customers only, with no comparison to customers who stayed. Since 80% of those churned customers got the price notice, it is weaker evidence than the account data.
- **Data-quality issue:** accounts that signed up from August to December 2025 are marked as having received the "July 2025" notice at the same rate as earlier signups. It's worth checking what that column really means before acting on it.

**Recommendation:** keep a small onboarding project you can measure, such as an A/B test of the checklist, and move most of next quarter's effort to accounts that got the price notice. I've written this as advice rather than a change to the plan, since engineering time is already reserved.

I fixed issue #12: `summary` now reads the log one line at a time, so its memory use no longer grows with the file size. On a 290 MB test log its peak traced memory dropped from about 766 MB to about 145 KB. All tests pass.

**Cause:** `logstat/reader.py` loaded the whole file into memory and then split it into a list of lines. On a 2 GB log that comes to several GB, which caused the MemoryError.

**What I changed:**
- **`logstat/reader.py`:** `read_all` now hands back lines one at a time instead of building a list. Its output is the same (line endings removed) and it keeps the same name.
- **Issues #15 and #19:** `tail` and `grep` also read the whole file at once, which is the same cause as these two open issues, so I fixed them too. `tail` now keeps only the last N lines in memory. `grep` streams through the file and returns its matches as it goes. Both show the same output as before.
- **`tests/test_logstat.py`:** I added a regression test that fails if `read_all` goes back to loading the whole file.

**How I checked it:**
- `python -m unittest discover -s tests` passes all 5 tests (the 4 existing ones plus the new one).
- On a generated 290 MB log with 4.5 million lines, peak traced memory was:

| Command | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| summary | about 766 MB | about 145 KB |
| tail | not measured | about 147 KB |
| grep | not measured | about 146 KB |

  The counts, the last line and the grep match were all correct. Time on that file was about 15 s for summary, 4 s for tail and 6 s for grep.
- I didn't have the real 2 GB production log, so the fix hasn't been tried on it.

**One small difference:** lines are now split only on `\n`, `\r` and `\r\n`. Before, some unusual characters such as form feed (`\x0c`) or the Unicode line separator also started a new line. Normal log files won't notice.

Issue #12 is fixed: `python -m logstat summary` no longer runs out of memory on large logs. I generated a 2.1 GB log and ran `summarize` on it. It counted all 60M lines correctly and peak traced memory stayed around 145 KB. It took about 140 s.

**Cause:** `summary` calls `read_all()` in `logstat/reader.py`, and that function read the whole file into one string and then split it into a list of lines. On a 2 GB file that needs several GB of RAM.

**What I changed:**
- **`logstat/reader.py`:** `read_all()` now hands back lines one at a time as it reads the file, instead of returning a list. It splits lines by the same rules as the old version, so the results are the same. Its only caller is `summary`, which just loops over the lines, so nothing else had to change.
- **`tests/test_logstat.py`:** added `test_read_all_streams`, which checks that `read_all()` no longer returns a full list.

**Checks:**
- All 5 tests pass with `python -m unittest discover -s tests` (the 4 existing ones plus the new one).
- The 2 GB run above; I deleted the generated file afterwards.

**Not changed:** `ISSUES.md` lists two more crashes on big logs that have the same cause: #15 (`tail` uses `readlines()`) and #19 (`grep` uses `f.read()`). Neither command uses `read_all`, so this fix doesn't help them. I left them alone because they're separate tickets. Each needs a similar small change, plus keeping only the last N lines for `tail`.

The data doesn't support the idea that churn is mainly an onboarding problem. The biggest factor is the July 2025 price-increase notice.

| Group | Churn rate |
|---|---|
| Got the price notice | **34.2%** |
| Didn't get the notice | **5.2%** |
| Didn't finish onboarding | 17.6% |
| Finished onboarding | 15.2% |

- **Price notice:** 80% of the accounts that churned had received it. The gap shows up in every plan type and at every support-ticket level.
- **Onboarding:** the gap is only 2.4 points, and the 95% range of −0.3 to +5.0 includes zero. When I compare only accounts that got the notice, or only those that didn't, it stays at about 2 points.
- **What a perfect rebuild could achieve:** if every account had finished onboarding, churn would fall from 16.2% to about 15.3%. That is under 1 point, and only if the gap is entirely caused by onboarding.
- **Other columns:** plan, seats and signup month make little difference. Support tickets rise mostly among accounts that got the notice, so they look like a reaction to the price change rather than a separate cause.
- **Exit survey:** the "68% said onboarding was confusing" result has nothing to compare against. We don't know what retained customers would say, or how many churned customers answered.

These are correlations, not proof of cause, and there are two data problems. Accounts that signed up from August to December also show the "July 2025" notice, and the data has no churn dates, so I couldn't confirm churn came after the notice. Before engineering time is committed, I'd look at how the price increase was rolled out. If the onboarding rebuild goes ahead, run it with a holdout group so its effect gets measured.

pushguard now blocks `git push --force`, `git push -f` and `git push --force-with-lease`, and lets everything else through as before. All tests pass; nothing is committed.

**What changed**

`pushguard/guard.py`: `is_blocked` now splits the command line the way a shell would. It respects quotes and breaks on `;`, `&&`, `||`, `|`, `&`, newlines, `( )`, `$( )` and backticks, so it can find a force push anywhere in the line. A `git push` is blocked when it has:
- **The three flags you named:** `--force`, `-f` (also inside combined flags like `-uf`), and `--force-with-lease` (with or without `=…`, or shortened as git allows, e.g. `--force-w`).
- **A `+` refspec:** for example `git push origin +main`. I added this one myself because it also overwrites the remote branch. Delete the `+refspec` check in `_push_args_force` if you'd rather allow it.

It still catches the push when the command is written in other ways: inside `bash -c '…'` or `sh -c '…'`, behind `sudo`, `env` or `VAR=1`, with git options before `push` (`git -C dir`, `git -c k=v`), or with a full or `.exe` path to git.

To keep other commands running as before, it does not block:
- Text that only looks like a force push, such as `git commit -m 'git push --force'` or `echo git push -f`.
- `-f` on other commands (`git fetch -f`, `git pull --force`, `rm -f`).
- The value after `-o`/`--push-option`, which is not a flag.
- Anything after `--`.
- A force flag cancelled later in the same command (`--no-force`, `--no-force-with-lease`).
- `--force-if-includes` on its own, since git ignores it without `--force-with-lease`.

If the quotes in a line don't match, it falls back to splitting on spaces rather than letting the line through unchecked.

**Limits:** it can't see through git aliases (e.g. a `git pf` alias for `push -f`) or scripts that push from inside. A lone quoted `";"` is read as a command break, so it may block a harmless line now and then; it errs toward blocking.

**How I checked it**
